topics.title: 1. Percentages & Fraction Conversion Table
topics.rawHtml:
1. Percentages & Fraction Equivalents

Memorizing key fraction-to-percentage conversions saves up to 40 seconds per arithmetic question.

FractionPercentageFractionPercentage
1/250%1/714.28%
1/333.33%1/812.50%
1/425%1/911.11%
1/520%1/1010%
1/616.67%1/128.33%
Successive Percentage Change: Net % = a + b + (a × b)/100
Note: Use negative values for decreases/discounts.
Expenditure Constant Trick: If price rises by x%, consumption must decrease by [x / (100 + x)] × 100% to keep expenditure unchanged.
topics.plainText: 1. Percentages & Fraction Equivalents 1/2=50%, 1/3=33.33%, 1/4=25%, 1/5=20%, 1/6=16.67%, 1/7=14.28%, 1/8=12.5%, 1/9=11.11%, 1/12=8.33%. Successive Percentage Change: Net = a + b + (a*b)/100. Price-Expenditure: [x/(100+x)]*100% reduction.

topics.title: 2. Profit, Loss, Discount & False Weights
topics.rawHtml:
2. Profit, Loss & Marked Price

Profit %: [(SP - CP) / CP] × 100
Loss %: [(CP - SP) / CP] × 100
Selling Price with Profit: SP = CP × [(100 + P%) / 100]
Discount %: [(MP - SP) / MP] × 100
Relation between CP and MP: CP / MP = (100 - Discount%) / (100 + Profit%)
False Weights / Dishonest Dealer:
Profit % = [Error / (True Value - Error)] × 100%
Example: Using 900g instead of 1000g → Gain = [100 / 900] × 100% = 11.11%.
topics.plainText: 2. Profit, Loss & Marked Price. Profit % = [(SP-CP)/CP]*100. SP = CP * (100+P%)/100. Discount % = [(MP-SP)/MP]*100. CP/MP = (100-D%)/(100+P%). False Weight Gain % = [Error/(True Value - Error)] * 100%.

topics.title: 3. Simple & Compound Interest
topics.rawHtml:
3. Simple & Compound Interest (SI & CI)

Simple Interest (SI): SI = (P × R × T) / 100
Compound Amount (A): A = P × (1 + R/100)T
Compound Interest (CI): CI = A - P
CI - SI Difference Shortcuts:
• For 2 Years: Difference = P × (R / 100)2
• For 3 Years: Difference = P × (R / 100)2 × [(300 + R) / 100]
Compounding Half-Yearly: Rate = R/2, Time = 2T
Compounding Quarterly: Rate = R/4, Time = 4T
topics.plainText: 3. Simple & Compound Interest. SI = (P*R*T)/100. CI Amount = P(1+R/100)^T. 2-Year CI-SI Difference = P*(R/100)^2. 3-Year CI-SI Difference = P*(R/100)^2 * [(300+R)/100]. Half-yearly: Rate/2, Time*2.

topics.title: 4. Ratio, Proportion & Variations
topics.rawHtml:
4. Ratio & Proportion

Mean Proportional between a and b: x = √(a × b)
Third Proportional to a and b: x = b2 / a
Fourth Proportional to a, b, c: x = (b × c) / a
Combining Ratios:
If A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5
Multiply to equalize B (LCM = 12): A : B : C = (2×4) : (3×4) : (3×5) = 8 : 12 : 15.
topics.plainText: 4. Ratio & Proportion. Mean proportional = sqrt(a*b). Third proportional = b^2/a. Fourth proportional = (b*c)/a. Combining ratios A:B and B:C via LCM of common term B.

topics.title: 5. Time, Speed & Distance, Trains & Boats
topics.rawHtml:
5. Time, Speed & Distance, Trains & Boats

Speed: Distance / Time
km/h to m/s conversion: Multiply by 5/18
m/s to km/h conversion: Multiply by 18/5
Average Speed (equal distance at speeds x and y): 2xy / (x + y)
Trains Crossing Scenarios:
• Train crossing Pole/Person: Distance = Length of Train (LT)
• Train crossing Platform/Bridge: Distance = LT + LPlatform
• Opposite directions: Relative speed = S1 + S2
• Same direction: Relative speed = |S1 - S2|
Boats & Streams:
Downstream Speed (D) = u + v | Upstream Speed (U) = u - v
Speed in Still Water (u) = (D + U) / 2 | Stream Speed (v) = (D - U) / 2
topics.plainText: 5. Time, Speed & Distance. Speed = D/T. km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. Avg speed for equal distance: 2xy/(x+y). Train crossing platform: D = L_train + L_platform. Relative speed: S1+S2 opposite, S1-S2 same. Boats: Downstream = u+v, Upstream = u-v. Still water speed = (D+U)/2, Stream = (D-U)/2.

topics.title: 6. Time, Work & Pipes/Cisterns
topics.rawHtml:
6. Time & Work Formulas

Chain Rule: (M1 × D1 × H1) / W1 = (M2 × D2 × H2) / W2
Two Workers Combined: If A takes x days and B takes y days → Combined = (x × y) / (x + y) days
LCM Efficiency Method:
Assume total work = LCM of individual times.
Example: A takes 12 days, B takes 18 days. Total work = 36 units. Efficiency A = 3 u/d, B = 2 u/d. Together = 36 / 5 = 7.2 days.
Pipes & Cisterns: Inlet rate is (+), Outlet/Leak rate is (-).
Net rate = (1/A + 1/B - 1/C) per hour.
topics.plainText: 6. Time & Work. Chain Rule: (M1*D1*H1)/W1 = (M2*D2*H2)/W2. Combined time: (x*y)/(x+y). LCM Efficiency Method: Total Work = LCM of times. Inlet/Outlet net rate: 1/A + 1/B - 1/C.

topics.title: 7. Mixtures & Allegations
topics.rawHtml:
7. Alligation & Repeated Dilution

Rule of Alligation:
(Quantity of Cheaper) / (Quantity of Dearer) = (Price of Dearer - Mean Price) / (Mean Price - Price of Cheaper)
Repeated Dilution Formula:
If a container holds C units of pure liquid and x units are drawn and replaced by water n times:
Final Quantity of Pure Liquid = C × [1 - (x / C)]n
topics.plainText: 7. Mixtures & Alligations. Cheaper/Dearer = (Dearer Price - Mean) / (Mean - Cheaper Price). Repeated Replacement: Final pure liquid = C * (1 - x/C)^n.

topics.title: 8. Number Systems, Divisibility & Unit Digits
topics.rawHtml:
8. Number Systems & Divisibility

DivisorCondition
3 / 9Sum of all digits is divisible by 3 or 9
4 / 8Last 2 digits divisible by 4 / Last 3 digits divisible by 8
6Divisible by both 2 (even) and 3
11Difference between (sum of odd placed digits) and (sum of even placed digits) is 0 or multiple of 11
Product of Two Numbers: HCF × LCM = Product of the Two Numbers
Cyclicity of Unit Digits (mod 4):
• 2, 3, 7, 8 have cyclicity of 4 (Divide power by 4, use remainder).
• 4, 9 have cyclicity of 2 (4odd=4, 4even=6; 9odd=9, 9even=1).
• 0, 1, 5, 6 always end in 0, 1, 5, 6 respectively.
topics.plainText: 8. Number Systems & Divisibility. Divisibility for 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11. HCF * LCM = Product of Two Numbers. Unit digit cyclicity: 2,3,7,8 (cycle 4), 4,9 (cycle 2), 0,1,5,6 (cycle 1).

topics.title: 9. Permutations, Combinations & Probability
topics.rawHtml:
9. Permutations & Combinations (P&C)

Permutations (Order matters): nPr = n! / (n - r)!
Combinations (Selection only): nCr = n! / [r! × (n - r)!]
Circular Arrangement: (n - 1)! (or (n - 1)! / 2 for necklaces/garlands)
Identical Items Arrangement: n! / (p! × q! × r!)
Probability: P(Event) = Desired Outcomes / Total Outcomes
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B)
For independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
P(at least one success) = 1 - P(zero successes)
topics.plainText: 9. Permutations & Combinations. nPr = n!/(n-r)!. nCr = n!/[r!(n-r)!]. Circular arrangement = (n-1)!. Probability = Desired/Total. P(A union B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A cap B). At least one = 1 - P(none).

topics.title: 1. Clocks & Angle Formulas
topics.rawHtml:
1. Clocks & Angle Calculations

Angle between Hour and Minute Hand:
θ = |30 × H - (11 / 2) × M|
Example at 4:20: θ = |30(4) - 5.5(20)| = |120 - 110| = 10°.
Critical Key Clock Facts:
• Minute hand moves 6° per minute (360° / 60 min).
• Hour hand moves 0.5° per minute (360° / 720 min).
• Relative speed of minute hand over hour hand = 5.5° per minute (11/2°).
• Coincide (0°): 22 times in 24 hours.
• Opposite (180°): 22 times in 24 hours.
• Right angles (90°): 44 times in 24 hours.
topics.plainText: 1. Clocks & Angles. Angle = |30*H - 5.5*M|. Minute hand = 6 deg/min, Hour hand = 0.5 deg/min. Relative speed = 5.5 deg/min. Coincide 22 times/day, Opposite 22 times/day, Right angle 44 times/day.

topics.title: 2. Calendars & Odd Days System
topics.rawHtml:
2. Calendars & Odd Days Calculation

An 'odd day' is the remainder left when total days are divided by 7.

PeriodOdd Days
Ordinary Year (365 days)1 odd day
Leap Year (366 days)2 odd days
100 Years5 odd days
200 Years3 odd days
300 Years1 odd day
400 Years (Century Leap)0 odd days
Day Codes: 0 = Sunday, 1 = Monday, 2 = Tuesday, 3 = Wednesday, 4 = Thursday, 5 = Friday, 6 = Saturday.
Calendar Repetition:
• Leap Year: Repeats after 28 years.
• Year immediately after leap year (e.g. 2021 after 2020): Repeats after 6 years.
• Other ordinary years: Repeat after 11 years.
topics.plainText: 2. Calendars & Odd Days. Normal year = 1 odd day. Leap year = 2 odd days. 100 yrs = 5, 200 yrs = 3, 300 yrs = 1, 400 yrs = 0. Calendar repetition: Leap = 28 yrs, Leap+1 = 6 yrs, Others = 11 yrs.

topics.title: 3. Seating Arrangement Golden Rules
topics.rawHtml:
3. Seating Arrangement Strategies

Step-by-Step Solving Approach:
1. Anchor Selection: Begin with 100% definite clues (e.g., 'A sits at the extreme left end' or 'B sits opposite to C').
2. Direction Awareness:
• Facing North: Left is West (←), Right is East (→).
• Facing South: Left is East (→), Right is West (←).
• Circular Facing Center: Clockwise is Left, Anti-clockwise is Right.
• Circular Facing Outward: Clockwise is Right, Anti-clockwise is Left.
3. Use Multiple Cases: When a clue offers two possibilities (e.g., B is 2nd to left or right), maintain two parallel sketches and eliminate the contradiction later.
topics.plainText: 3. Seating Arrangement Strategies. Anchor selection: start with definite positions. Facing North (Left=West, Right=East). Facing South (Left=East, Right=West). Center-facing circle (Clockwise=Left, Anti-clockwise=Right). Outward-facing circle (Clockwise=Right, Anti-clockwise=Left).

topics.title: 4. Blood Relations & Generation Mapping
topics.rawHtml:
4. Blood Relations Representation

Family Tree Notation Standards:
• [ + ] = Male | [ - ] = Female
• [ = ] = Married Couple (Spouses)
• [ — ] = Siblings (Brother/Sister)
• [ | ] = Vertical generation descent (Parent above, Child below)
Common Trap: Do NOT assume a person's gender from their name! Always verify gender strictly from pronouns ('he', 'she') or explicit relationship words ('father', 'sister', 'daughter').
topics.plainText: 4. Blood Relations. Notation: [+] Male, [-] Female, [=] Spouses, [--] Siblings, [|] Parent-child generation. Caution: Never assume gender from a name alone.

topics.title: 5. Syllogisms & Venn Deduction Logic
topics.rawHtml:
5. Syllogisms Deduction Rules

Statement TypeMeaningDefinite Conversion
All A are BA is completely inside BSome B are A
Some A are BA and B overlapSome B are A
No A is BA and B completely separateNo B is A
Only a few A are BSome A are B AND Some A are not BSome B are A
Either-Or Complementary Pair Conditions:
Both conclusions must be uncertain individually, have the same subject and predicate, and form one of the pairs:
1. 'Some' + 'No'
2. 'All' + 'Some not'
topics.plainText: 5. Syllogisms. All A are B implies Some B are A. No A is B implies No B is A. 'Only a few' implies Some are and Some are not. Either-Or requires complementary pairs (Some + No, All + Some not) with common terms.

topics.title: 6. Order and Ranking Formulas
topics.rawHtml:
6. Order and Ranking Cheat Sheet

Total Persons in a Row: Total = (Left + Right) - 1
Position from Right: Right = (Total - Left) + 1
Interchanging Positions:
Total = (New position of A + Old position of B) - 1
Overlapping Case (When Left + Right > Total):
Persons between = (Left + Right) - Total - 2
Non-Overlapping Case (When Left + Right < Total):
Persons between = Total - (Left + Right)
topics.plainText: 6. Order & Ranking. Total = Left + Right - 1. Right = Total - Left + 1. Overlapping between = (Left + Right) - Total - 2. Non-overlapping between = Total - (Left + Right).

topics.title: 7. Coding-Decoding & Opposite Letter Pairs
topics.rawHtml:
7. Alphabetical Positions & Opposite Pairs

EJOTY Rule: E(5), J(10), O(15), T(20), Y(25)
VQLG Rule (Reverse): Z(26), Y(25)... A(1)
Opposite Letters Memory Mnemonics (Sum = 27):
A - Z (AZad) | B - Y (BYe) | C - X (CruX) | D - W (Dew / Door-Window)
E - V (EVening) | F - U (FUll) | G - T (GT Road) | H - S (High School)
I - R (Indian Railways) | J - Q (Jungle Queen) | K - P (Kurta Pajama)
L - O (LOve) | M - N (MaN)
topics.plainText: 7. Coding-Decoding. EJOTY = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Opposite pairs sum to 27: AZ, BY, CX, DW, EV, FU, GT, HS, IR, JQ, KP, LO, MN.

topics.title: 8. Inequalities Decision Flow
topics.rawHtml:
8. Inequalities Golden Rules

Precedence of Signs:
Priority 1: > or <
Priority 2: ≥ or ≤
Priority 3: =
Opposing Signs Break the Relation:
If A > B < C, or A ≤ B ≥ C, NO definite relationship can be established between A and C.
Conclusion is either false or requires an Either-Or pair (A > C or A ≤ C).
topics.plainText: 8. Inequalities. Precedence: > / < beats >= / <= beats =. Opposing signs (> and <) block definite comparison; relationship between extremities cannot be determined.

topics.title: 1. Subject-Verb Agreement Essentials
topics.rawHtml:
1. Subject-Verb Agreement Top 5 Rules

Rule 1: Proximity Rule (Either/Or, Neither/Nor):
Verb agrees with the subject closest to it.
• Neither the CEO nor the engineers were present.
• Neither the engineers nor the CEO was present.
Rule 2: Parenthetical Expressions:
Words like 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with', 'accompanied by', 'in addition to' do NOT alter the number of the subject.
• The lead architect, along with his entire team, is deploying the patch (singular).
Rule 3: Indefinite Pronouns:
Each, Everyone, Somebody, Nobody, Either, Neither take singular verbs.
• Each of the microservices has its own database instance.
topics.plainText: 1. Subject-Verb Agreement. Either/Or agrees with closer subject. 'Along with' / 'as well as' does not change subject number. Each, everyone, neither take singular verbs.

topics.title: 2. Conditional Sentences & Tense Structures
topics.rawHtml:
2. Conditional Clauses (If-Then Matrix)

TypeCondition Clause ('If')Main Clause
ZeroSimple PresentSimple Present (Universal truth)
FirstSimple Presentwill / can / may + Base Verb
SecondSimple Pastwould / could / might + Base Verb
ThirdPast Perfect (had + V3)would have / could have + V3
Inversion Trap in Third Conditional:
'If he had known' → 'Had he known'.
Correct: 'Had the team run unit tests, the bug would have been caught.' (Do NOT write 'Had they had run').
topics.plainText: 2. Conditional Sentences. Zero (Present -> Present). First (Present -> will+verb). Second (Past -> would+verb). Third (had+V3 -> would have+V3). Inversion: 'Had he known...'.

topics.title: 3. Dangling & Misplaced Modifiers
topics.rawHtml:
3. Dangling & Misplaced Modifiers

The Golden Rule: An introductory descriptive phrase must immediately precede the noun that actually performs the action.
Incorrect: Walking into the server room, the cold air chilled Raman.
(Was the cold air walking into the room? No!)
Correct: Walking into the server room, Raman felt chilled by the cold air.
topics.plainText: 3. Dangling Modifiers. Introductory participle phrases must immediately modify the doer of the action. Incorrect: Walking to office, rain fell. Correct: Walking to office, I got wet.

topics.title: 4. Parallelism in Sentence Correction
topics.rawHtml:
4. Parallelism & Correlative Conjunctions

Items in a list or connected by correlative conjunctions must share identical grammatical form.

Correlative Pairs: Not only... but also | Either... or | Neither... nor | Both... and
Incorrect: She likes coding, designing, and to deploy microservices.
Correct: She likes coding, designing, and deploying microservices.
Ensure the element following 'Not only' grammatically mirrors the element following 'but also' (Verb with Verb, Noun with Noun).
topics.plainText: 4. Parallelism. Elements joined by and/or/not only...but also must match in grammatical structure (all gerunds, all infinitives, or all nouns).

topics.title: 5. Active vs Passive Voice & Indirect Speech
topics.rawHtml:
5. Voice & Narration Shift Rules

Tense Shift in Reported Speech (Past Reporting Verb):
• Simple Present → Simple Past
• Present Continuous → Past Continuous
• Simple Past → Past Perfect
• Can → Could | Will → Would | May → Might
Universal scientific truths do NOT change tense in indirect speech.
Example: He said, 'The earth revolves around the sun' → He said that the earth revolves around the sun.
topics.plainText: 5. Voice & Speech. Simple Present -> Simple Past. Simple Past -> Past Perfect. Will -> Would, Can -> Could. Universal truths remain in present tense.

topics.title: 1. Bitwise Operators & Bit Shifting
topics.rawHtml:
1. Bitwise Operators Cheat Sheet

OperatorNameOperationKey Property
&AND1 only if both bits 1x & 0 = 0 | x & 1 = x
|OR1 if either bit 1x | 0 = x | x | 1 = 1
^XOR1 if bits are differentx ^ x = 0 | x ^ 0 = x
~NOTInverts all bits~x = -(x + 1)
<< kLeft ShiftShifts bits left by kMultiplies by 2k
>> kRight ShiftShifts bits right by kDivides by 2k (floor)
Infosys Trick:
• x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit. If (x & (x - 1)) == 0, x is a power of 2!
• x ^ y without carry is used in parity checks and finding unique single numbers.
topics.plainText: 1. Bitwise Operators. AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~ = -(x+1)), Left shift << k (multiply by 2^k), Right shift >> k (divide by 2^k). x & (x-1) clears lowest set bit.

topics.title: 2. Loop Tracing Table Technique
topics.rawHtml:
2. Systematic Loop Tracing

To avoid silly off-by-one errors, always sketch a 4-column trace table:

IterationCondition CheckedState VariablesOutput / Print
1i ≤ 3 (1 ≤ 3 → True)a = 2, i = 2-
2i ≤ 3 (2 ≤ 3 → True)a = 4, i = 3-
3i ≤ 3 (3 ≤ 3 → True)a = 8, i = 4-
Exiti ≤ 3 (4 ≤ 3 → False)Loop terminatesPrint(a) = 8
Watch for Prefix vs Postfix increments:
• ++x: Increments first, returns new value.
• x++: Returns current value, increments afterwards.
topics.plainText: 2. Systematic Loop Tracing. Maintain columns: Iteration, Condition, State Variables, Output. Differentiate prefix (++x) vs postfix (x++).

topics.title: 3. Recursion & Stack Frames
topics.rawHtml:
3. Recursion Evaluation

Two Essential Components:
1. Base Case: Prevents infinite recursion (e.g. if (n ≤ 1) return 1).
2. Recursive Step: Shrinks problem towards the base case (e.g. return n * fact(n - 1)).
Tree vs Linear Recursion:
If a function calls itself twice (like fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)), sketch a small tree structure downwards, then sum values upward on the unwinding phase.
topics.plainText: 3. Recursion. Base case stops execution; recursive call reduces input. Trace call tree downwards to base case, then unwind returns back up.

topics.title: 4. Short-Circuit Evaluation & Operator Precedence
topics.rawHtml:
4. Short-Circuit Logic & Precedence

Short-Circuit Rules:
• In A && B: If A is FALSE, B is never evaluated.
• In A || B: If A is TRUE, B is never evaluated.
Example: if (x == 0 || ++y > 5) → If x is 0, y is NOT incremented!
Standard Precedence Hierarchy:
Parentheses () → Postfix ++/-- → Prefix ++/-- → Multiplicative (*, /, %) → Additive (+, -) → Relational (<, >) → Equality (==, !=) → Bitwise (&, ^, |) → Logical (&&, ||) → Assignment (=)
topics.plainText: 4. Short-Circuit & Precedence. A && B skips B if A is False. A || B skips B if A is True. Precedence: () -> ++/-- -> */% -> +/- -> comparisons -> logical -> assignment.

topics.title: 1. Data Sufficiency 5-Step Elimination
topics.rawHtml:
1. Data Sufficiency Solving Strategy

Standard Answer Choices:
(A) Statement I alone is sufficient, but II alone is not.
(B) Statement II alone is sufficient, but I alone is not.
(C) Statements I and II TOGETHER are sufficient.
(D) Statements I and II together are NOT sufficient.
(E) EACH statement alone is sufficient.
Elimination Protocol (12-D Method):
• Evaluate Statement I alone. If YES, answer is (A) or (E). If NO, answer is (B), (C), or (D).
• Evaluate Statement II alone. If YES, answer is (B) or (E). If NO, answer is (C) or (D).
• Only combine I and II if BOTH failed independently.
topics.plainText: 1. Data Sufficiency. Evaluate Statement 1 alone. Evaluate Statement 2 alone. Combine both only if neither works independently. Never bring outside unstated assumptions.

topics.title: 2. Statement and Assumptions
topics.rawHtml:
2. Identifying Implicit Assumptions

An assumption is unstated premise that the speaker/author MUST believe for the argument to hold validity.
Negation Test: Negate the assumption. If the original statement collapses or becomes illogical, the assumption is IMPLICIT.
Red Flag Words: Words like 'all', 'every', 'never', 'only', 'impossible' indicate extreme assumptions that are usually NOT implicit unless explicitly justified.
topics.plainText: 2. Statement & Assumptions. An assumption is implicit if negating it destroys the core statement. Avoid extreme assumptions containing 'all', 'only', 'never'.

topics.title: 3. Statement and Course of Action
topics.rawHtml:
3. Course of Action Guidelines

Criteria for a Valid Course of Action:
1. Feasibility: Is it realistic and practically executable?
2. Direct Problem Mitigation: Does it directly tackle the issue stated?
3. Proportionality: The action must NOT be excessively harsh or create a worse problem than the original one.
topics.plainText: 3. Course of Action. Must be practically feasible, proportional to severity, and directly resolve the problem without causing worse unintended consequences.

topics.title: 2. Three-Pass Examination Strategy
topics.rawHtml:
2. The Three-Pass Strategy

Pass 1 (0 – 35 min): Direct Confidence Hits
Answer all direct formula-based quant, vocabulary, grammar corrections, and straightforward reasoning questions. Skip long puzzles or complex code tracing immediately.
Pass 2 (35 – 75 min): Medium Complexity & Arrangements
Solve multi-step math problems, seating arrangements, syllogisms, and line-by-line pseudocode.
Pass 3 (75 – 90 min): Challenging Puzzles & Final Review
Tackle complex multi-variable floor/box puzzles, verify boundary conditions, and ensure 0 questions remain unanswered.
topics.plainText: 2. Three-Pass Strategy. Pass 1: Quick 30-sec direct questions. Pass 2: Medium calculation & standard logic. Pass 3: Long puzzles, difficult pseudocode, final checks.
